{{Short description|Intrinsic instability in flames}}
The '''Darrieus–Landau instability''', or '''density fingering''', refers to an instability of chemical fronts propagating into a denser medium, named after [[Georges Jean Marie Darrieus]] and [[Lev Landau]].<ref>{{cite journal|last=Darrieus, G.|title=Propagation d'un front de flamme|journal=La Technique Moderne and Congrés de Mécanique Appliquée Paris|year=1938}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Landau, L. D.|title=On the theory of slow combustion|journal=Acta Physicochim.|year=1944}}</ref> It is a key [[Combustion instability#Classification of combustion instabilities|instrinsic flame instability]] that occurs in [[premixed flame]]s, caused by density variations due to [[thermal expansion]] of the gas produced by the [[combustion]] process. In simple terms, stability inquires whether a steadily propagating plane sheet with a discontinuous jump in density is stable or not. 

The analysis behind the Darrieus–Landau instability considers a planar, premixed [[flame]] front subjected to very small perturbations.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Combustion Waves and Fronts in Flows|last1=Clavin|first1=Paul|last2=Searby|first2=Geoff|date=2016|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=9781316162453|location=Cambridge|doi=10.1017/cbo9781316162453}}</ref> It is useful to think of this arrangement as one in which the unperturbed flame is stationary, with the reactants (fuel and oxidizer) directed towards the flame and perpendicular to it with a velocity u1, and the burnt gases leaving the flame also in a perpendicular way but with velocity u2. The analysis assumes that the flow is [[incompressible flow|incompressible]], and that perturbations are governed by the linearized [[Euler equations]], and are thus inviscid.

With these considerations, the main result of this analysis is that, if the density of burnt [[gases]] is less than that of the reactants (true in practice due to thermal expansion of the gas produced by combustion), the flame front is unstable to perturbations of any [[wavelength]]. Another result is that the rate of growth of perturbations is inversely proportional to their wavelength; thus small flames (but larger than the characteristic flame thickness) tend to wrinkle, and grow faster than larger ones. In practice, however, diffusive and buoyancy effects that are not taken into account by the analysis of Darrieus and Landau may have a stabilizing effect.<ref>Markstein, G. H. Non-steady flame Propagation,(1964). ''P22, Pergarmon, New York''.</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Frankel|first1=M. L.|last2=Sivashinsky|first2=G. I.|date=December 1982|title=The Effect of Viscosity on Hydrodynamic Stability of a Plane Flame Front|journal=Combustion Science and Technology|volume=29|issue=3–6|pages=207–224|doi=10.1080/00102208208923598|issn=0010-2202}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Matalon|first1=M.|last2=Matkowsky|first2=B. J.|date=November 1982|title=Flames as gasdynamic discontinuities|journal=Journal of Fluid Mechanics|volume=124|pages=239–259|doi=10.1017/S0022112082002481|issn=1469-7645|bibcode=1982JFM...124..239M|s2cid=121744586 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Pelce|first1=P.|last2=Clavin|first2=P.|date=November 1982|title=Influence of hydrodynamics and diffusion upon the stability limits of laminar premixed flames|journal=Journal of Fluid Mechanics|volume=124|pages=219–237|doi=10.1017/S002211208200247X|issn=1469-7645|bibcode=1982JFM...124..219P|s2cid=102965398 }}</ref>

== History ==
[[Yakov Zeldovich]] notes that [[Lev Landau]] generously suggested this problem for him to investigate, and Zeldovich however, made calculation errors which led Landau himself to complete the work.<ref>Zeldovich, Ya. B. (1987) Remembering a teacher. For the Eightieth birthday of L. D. Landau: In: Selected Works of Yakov Borisovich Zeldovich, Volume II.</ref><ref>Zeldovich, Ya. B. (1989) Recollections of the teacher: In: Landau: the physicist & the man.</ref>

==Dispersion relation==
{{More footnotes needed|section|date=July 2023}}
If disturbances to the steady planar flame sheet are of the form <math>e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{x}_\bot+\sigma t}</math>, where <math>\mathbf{x}_\bot</math> is the transverse coordinate system that lies on the undisturbed stationary flame sheet, <math>t</math> is the time, <math>\mathbf{k}</math> is the wavevector of the disturbance and <math>\sigma</math> is the temporal growth rate of the disturbance, then the dispersion relation is given by<ref>Williams, F. A. (2018). Combustion theory. CRC Press. page 353</ref>

:<math>\frac{\sigma}{S_L k} = \frac{r}{r+1}\left(\sqrt{1+ \frac{r^2-1}{r}}-1\right) </math>

where <math>S_L</math> is the laminar burning velocity (or, the [[flow velocity]] far upstream of the flame in a frame that is fixed to the flame), <math>k=|\mathbf{k}|</math> and <math>r=\rho_u/\rho_b</math> is the ratio of burnt to unburnt gas density. In combustion, <math>r>1</math> always and therefore the growth rate <math>\sigma>0</math> for all wavenumbers. This implies that a plane sheet of flame with a burning velocity <math>S_L</math> is unstable for all wavenumbers. In fact, [[Amable Liñán]] and [[Forman A. Williams]] quote in their book<ref>Liñán, A., & Williams, F. A. (1993). Fundamental aspects of combustion.</ref><ref>Crighton, D. G. (1997). Fundamental Aspects of Combustion. By A. Liñan & FA Williams. Oxford University Press, 1993, 167 pp. {{ISBN|019507626 5}}.£ 25. Journal of Fluid Mechanics, 331, 439-443.</ref> that: "... ''in view of laboratory observations of stable, planar, laminar flames, publication of their theoretical predictions required courage on the part of Darrieus and Landau".''

=== With buoyancy ===
If buoyancy forces are taken into account (in others words, [[Rayleigh–Taylor instability]] is considered) for planar flames perpendicular to the gravity vector, then some stability can be anticipated for flames propagating vertically downwards (or flames held stationary by an upward flow), since in these cases, the denser unburnt gas lies beneath the lighter burnt gas mixture. Of course, for flames propagating upwards or those held stationary by downward flow, both the Darrieus–Landau mechanism and the Rayleigh–Taylor mechanism contributes to the destabilizing effect. The dispersion relation when buoyance forces are included becomes

:<math>\frac{\sigma}{S_L k} = \frac{r}{r+1}\left[\sqrt{1+ \left(\frac{r^2-1}{r}\right)\left(1-\frac{g}{S_L^2 r k }\right)}-1\right] </math>

where <math>g>0</math> corresponds to gravitational acceleration for flames propagating downwards and <math>g<0</math> corresponds to gravitational acceleration for flames propagating upwards. The above dispersion implies that gravity introduces stability for downward propagating flames when <math>k^{-1}>l_{b}=S_{L}^2r/g</math>, where <math>l_b</math> is a characteristic buoyancy [[length scale]]. For small values of <math>r-1</math>, the growth rate becomes

:<math>\frac{\sigma}{S_L k} =\frac{1}{2}(r-1)  +\cdots \quad k^{-1}\ll l_b,</math>
:<math>\frac{\sigma}{S_L k} =\frac{1}{2}(r-1) \left(1-\frac{g}{S_L^2 k}\right) +\cdots \quad k^{-1}\sim l_b,</math>
:<math>\frac{\sigma}{g/S_L} =-\frac{1}{2}(r-1) +\cdots \quad k^{-1}\gg l_b.</math>

===Limitations===
Darrieus and Landau's analysis treats the flame as a plane sheet to investigate its stability with the neglect of diffusion effects, whereas in reality, the flame has a definite thickness, say the laminar flame thickness <math>k^{-1}\sim \delta_L=D_T/S_L</math>, where <math>D_T</math> is the [[thermal diffusivity]], wherein diffusion effects cannot be neglected. Accounting for the [[flame structure]], as first envisioned by [[George H. Markstein]], is found to result in stabilized flames for small wavelengths <math>k^{-1}\sim \delta_L</math>, except when the fuel diffusion coefficient and thermal diffusivity differ from each other significantly, leading to the so-called ([[Turing pattern|Turing]]) [[Diffusive–thermal instability|diffusive-thermal instability]]. The full dispersion relation <math>\sigma=\sigma(k)</math> with diffusive-thermal stabilising effect is given by the [[Clavin–Garcia equation]].

Darrieus–Landau instability manifests in the range <math>\delta_L\ll k^{-1}\ll l_b</math> for downward propagating flames, and <math>\delta_L\ll k^{-1}</math> for upward propagating flames.

=== Under Darcy's law ===
The classical dispersion relation was based on the assumption that the hydrodynamics is governed by [[Euler equations (fluid dynamics)|Euler equations]]. In strongly confined systems such as a [[Hele-Shaw flow|Hele-Shaw cell]] or in porous media, hydrodynamics however, is governed by [[Darcy's law]]. The dispersion relation based on Darcy's law was derived by J. Daou and P. Rajamanickam,<ref>Rajamanickam, P., & Daou, J. (2024). Hydrodynamic theory of premixed flames under Darcy's law. Physics of Fluids, 36(12).</ref><ref>Daou, J., & Rajamanickam, P. (2025). Hydrodynamic instabilities of propagating interfaces under Darcy's law. Physical Review Fluids.</ref> and reads:

:<math>\frac{\sigma}{S_L k} = \frac{r-1}{1+m} + \frac{1-m}{1+m}\frac{V}{S_L} - \frac{r-1}{1+m}  \frac{\rho_b g\kappa_b}{S_L \mu_b}</math>

where <math>r = \rho_u/\rho_b>1</math> is the density ratio, <math>m=(\mu_u/\kappa_u)/(\mu_b/\kappa_b)<1</math> is the ratio of friction factor which involves viscosity <math>\mu</math> and permeability <math>\kappa</math> (in Hele-Shaw cells, <math>\kappa_u=\kappa_b=h^2/12</math>, where <math>h</math> is the cell width, so that <math>m=\mu_u/\mu_b</math> is simply the viscosity ratio). 

<math>V</math> is the speed of a uniform imposed flow. When <math>V>0</math>, the imposed flow opposes flame propagation and when <math>V<0</math>, it aids flame propagation.

As before, <math>g>0</math> corresponds to downward flame propagation and <math>g<0</math> to upward flame propagation. The three terms in the above formula, respectively, corresponds to Darrieus–Landau instability (density fingering), [[Saffman–Taylor instability]] (viscous fingering) and [[Rayleigh–Taylor instability]] (gravity fingering), all in the context of Darcy's law. The Saffman–Taylor instability is specific to confined flames and does not exist in unconfined flames.
